name: The Easterlin Paradox
statement: Within a country the rich are happier, yet growing richer over decades leaves a nation no happier.
meaning: The Easterlin paradox is the tension between two findings about money and happiness. At a single moment, richer people within a country report being happier than poorer ones, and richer nations tend to look happier than poorer ones. But over the long run, as a country's average income grows across decades, its average reported happiness does not rise. The cross-sectional picture and the long-run trend point in opposite directions, and that is the paradox.
mechanism: The leading explanations turn on comparison and adaptation. If happiness depends on income relative to others rather than its absolute level, then when everyone grows richer together no one's relative standing improves, so average happiness need not rise. The hedonic treadmill adds that people adjust to higher incomes, so the glow of gains fades as the new level becomes the baseline. Easterlin himself stressed rising aspirations: growth would raise happiness other things equal, but it also lifts material wants, and the two effects roughly cancel over the long run.

examples.tag: Rich versus poor within a country
examples.text: At any given time, higher-income people report more happiness than lower-income people, the cross-sectional half of the paradox that both sides largely accept.
Easterlin's 1974 data showed decades of rising national income unaccompanied by rising average happiness, the long-run half that is most disputed.
Using larger, newer datasets, Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers argued in 2008 that happiness does rise with income within and between countries and over time, with no clear satiation point.

variants.name: The relative-income account
variants.text: The view that wellbeing tracks one's income compared with a reference group, so uniform growth changes nothing, a central explanation for the flat long-run trend.

variants.name: Easterlin's defence
variants.text: Easterlin and colleagues' reply that critics conflate the short-run rise and fall of happiness over the business cycle with the flat long-run relationship, which they maintain holds.

whyItMatters: It is foundational to the economics of happiness and to debates over whether gross domestic product adequately measures a nation's progress. It underlies arguments for wellbeing-based policy metrics and for looking beyond growth, and it forces careful thought about what income does and does not buy, making it one of the most influential and most contested findings in the study of subjective wellbeing.

working.text: distinguish the cross-sectional link between income and happiness at a moment from the long-run trend as a country grows, which behave differently.
keep the short-run comovement of happiness with the business cycle separate from the decades-long trend, the crux of the dispute.
weigh which datasets and happiness scales are used, since the verdict shifts with older versus newer data and with how wellbeing is measured.

limits: It is genuinely contested, not settled. Stevenson and Wolfers, using broader and more recent data, found a robust positive link between income and wellbeing within and between countries and over time, challenging the paradox, especially its between-country and satiation claims; Easterlin and colleagues defend the long-run within-country claim as the durable core. The verdict depends heavily on the time horizon, the datasets, and how happiness is measured, so the finding is best labelled contested.
misreadings: It does not say money cannot buy happiness at all; at a given moment richer people are happier, a point both sides largely accept. The subtle claim is specifically about long-run national trends, not individuals. It is a disputed empirical regularity, not a proven law. And it should not be confused with the short-run link, since happiness does move with the business cycle even if the long-run trend is flat.
origin: Proposed by the economist Richard Easterlin in his 1974 paper 'Does Economic Growth Improve the Human Lot?', and sharply challenged by Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers in 2008, with Easterlin and colleagues defending it in 2010.

sources.text: Easterlin paradox, Wikipedia. — the point-in-time versus over-time findings, the explanations, and the Stevenson-Wolfers challenge.
Stevenson & Wolfers, "Economic Growth and Subjective Well-Being: Reassessing the Easterlin Paradox," NBER Working Paper 14282 (2008). — the reassessment finding a robust income-wellbeing link.
